opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and it's really central to why we started the company. The way I think about it, the core problem with AI risk right now is that we're building incredibly powerful systems that we fundamentally don't understand. We train these models, we see what they do on the outside, we can poke at them with evals and red-teaming, but what's actually happening inside the network is still largely a black box. And it's hard to make strong safety guarantees about something you can't see into.

So Goodfire's bet is that interpretability, actually understanding the internal representations and computations of these models, is one of the most important levers we have. If you can look inside a model and see the concepts it's using, see when it's reasoning about something deceptive, or notice that it's latched onto some spurious feature, that gives you a fundamentally different kind of assurance than just observing behavior.

But I think what's distinctive about how we approach it is that we don't see interpretability as purely an academic exercise. We think it needs to become a real engineering discipline, something that practitioners actually use day to day to debug models, steer them, and design them more intentionally. Part of our theory of change is that if interpretability tools are genuinely useful, if they help people build better models and not just safer ones, then they get adopted widely. And once they're adopted, they become part of the infrastructure of how AI gets built, and that's when you really get leverage on safety.

There's also a field-building piece. Interpretability has historically lived inside a handful of frontier labs, and a lot of the best work stays internal. We want to push the frontier of the research ourselves, but also make these tools accessible to researchers, companies, and developers more broadly, so more people can actually look inside the models they're working with.

Longer term, my hope is that we get to a world where we're not just training a model and hoping it turns out okay, but where we can actually understand and shape what it's learned. That's a much healthier position for humanity to be in as these systems get more capable, and I think interpretability is one of the most promising paths to get there.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the way I'd frame it is that the biggest lever we have on AI risk right now is actually understanding what's going on inside these models. Most of the discourse around safety has been about behavior, you know, you put a prompt in, you look at what comes out, and you try to shape that with training. And that's important, but it's fundamentally a black-box approach. You're treating the model like a mysterious organism and hoping that the behavior you see in testing generalizes to the behavior you'll see in deployment.

What we're trying to do at Goodfire is make that not a black box anymore. The bet is that interpretability, the science of actually reading and editing the internal representations of a model, is going to become a core part of how you build and deploy these systems safely. If you can see the features a model is using when it makes a decision, you can catch things that would never show up in an eval. You can see when a model is representing something like deception or sycophancy internally, even if the output looks fine. And more than just seeing it, you can intervene. You can steer it, turn things up or down, and verify that the intervention actually did what you think it did.

So our role, concretely, is to take the research that's been happening in labs, things like sparse autoencoders and feature-level analysis, and turn it into tools that people building with these models can actually use. Because right now a lot of that work lives in papers, and the gap between a paper and something a developer can pick up and put in their pipeline is enormous. We want to close that gap.

And I'd add one more thing, which is that I think there's a real risk of interpretability staying a niche academic thing while the models keep getting more capable. If the tooling doesn't keep pace with capabilities, then by the time it really matters, we won't have the infrastructure to look inside the systems we've built. So part of what we're doing is just trying to make sure that the understanding side of this keeps up with the scaling side.

astra-6.text:
I think Goodfire’s role is to help make these systems more understandable and more steerable. Right now, we largely evaluate models by looking at what they do: you give them inputs, observe the outputs, and try to infer whether they’re behaving safely. That’s necessary, but it leaves a lot of uncertainty about what’s happening underneath.

The promise of mechanistic interpretability is that we can start looking inside the model and understanding the mechanisms that produce its behavior. If a model does something concerning, can we understand why? Can we identify the relevant internal representations and intervene in a way that reliably improves the behavior?

I wouldn’t frame that as a complete solution to AI risk. You still need evaluations, security, and thoughtful deployment decisions. But I think understanding the systems we’re building is a foundational capability. Our role is to help turn that understanding into practical tools, so that safety depends less on trial and error and more on knowing what we’re actually changing.

sol-6.1.text:
I see Goodfire’s role as helping us understand what’s happening inside AI models well enough to make them safer and more reliable. Today, we can evaluate a model’s behavior, but that only gives us a partial picture. A model can perform well on a test without us understanding why—or knowing when that behavior might change.

Interpretability offers a way to get additional evidence: what concepts a model is representing, what’s driving a particular response, and whether we can intervene when something goes wrong. The ambition is to turn that understanding into practical tools for finding problems and steering models more precisely.

I wouldn’t frame interpretability as a complete solution to AI risk. We need to demonstrate that our explanations are faithful and that our interventions actually work. But I think making these systems less opaque can give the people building and deploying them a much stronger basis for making safety decisions.
